description.en: Fractions, decimals, powers of ten, metric conversions, compound shapes and word problems.

html.en: Simplify = divide the top and the bottom by the same number until you can't any more. The biggest number that divides both is the highest common factor.

Simplify 24/36
24 ÷ 12 = 2    36 ÷ 12 = 3  →  2/3
Not sure of the HCF? Halve step by step: 24/36 → 12/18 → 6/9 → 2/3. Same answer.
Compare two fractions by giving them the same denominator, then just look at the numerators. Same-denominator fractions are easy: bigger top = bigger fraction.

Which is bigger, 5/9 or 2/3?
Common denominator 9:   2/3 = 6/9
5/9 vs 6/9 → 5 < 6, so  5/9 < 2/3
Fast trick — cross multiply. For a/b vs c/d, compare a×d against c×b. 5/9 vs 2/3 → 5×3 = 15 and 2×9 = 18. 15 < 18, so 5/9 < 2/3.
Careful: a bigger denominator does not mean a bigger fraction. 1/10 is much smaller than 1/2 — more slices means smaller slices.
Adding & subtracting — you MUST have the same denominator first. Find a common denominator, convert both fractions, then add or subtract the tops only. The bottom never changes.

3/8 + 1/6
Common denominator of 8 and 6 → 24
3/8 = 9/24    1/6 = 4/24
9/24 + 4/24 = 13/24  (already simplest)
Multiplying — no common denominator needed! Tops × tops, bottoms × bottoms, then simplify.

3/4 × 8/9
3 × 8 = 24    4 × 9 = 36  →  24/36
Simplify: 24/36 = 2/3
Dividing — Keep, Change, Flip. Keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, flip the second fraction upside down. Then multiply as normal.

4/5 ÷ 2/3
Keep 4/5 · Change ÷ to × · Flip 2/3 → 3/2
4/5 × 3/2 = 12/10 = 6/5 = 1 1/5
The two classic errors: finding a common denominator before multiplying (unnecessary), and forgetting to flip when dividing (fatal).
Mixed → improper: multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, keep the same denominator.  (bottom × side + top)

5 2/3 → improper
5 × 3 = 15    15 + 2 = 17
Answer: 17/3
Improper → mixed: divide the top by the bottom. The answer is the whole number, the remainder is the new numerator, the denominator stays the same.

41/6 → mixed
41 ÷ 6 = 6 remainder 5
Answer: 6 5/6
Check yourself instantly: 6 5/6 back to improper is 6×6+5 = 41 → 41/6 ✓ Every conversion can be checked in five seconds. Do it.
An improper fraction is always 1 or more — the top is bigger than (or equal to) the bottom. If your "improper" fraction is smaller than 1, you've made a mistake.
Multiplying: ignore the decimal points, multiply as whole numbers, then count how many decimal digits were in the question altogether — the answer has exactly that many.

12.6 × 4.3
Ignore points: 126 × 43 = 5418
Decimal digits: 12.6 has 1, 4.3 has 1 → total 2
Put 2 decimal places back: 54.18
Dividing by a whole number: use short division and keep the decimal point in the answer directly above the one in the question.

48.24 ÷ 8
48 ÷ 8 = 6  ·  2 ÷ 8 = 0 remainder 2  ·  24 ÷ 8 = 3
Answer: 6.03  (don't lose that zero!)
Estimate first, every time. 12.6 × 4.3 is roughly 13 × 4 = 52. If you got 5.418 or 541.8 you'd instantly know the point is in the wrong place.
Zeros matter. 48.24 ÷ 8 = 6.03, not 6.3. Write the placeholder zero.
Nothing moves the decimal point — the digits move. × 10 → 1 place left  ·  × 100 → 2 places left  ·  × 1,000 → 3 places left. Dividing moves them the same number of places to the right.

9.3 ÷ 100
2 places right: 9.3 → 0.93 → 0.093  (add zeros as placeholders)
Sense check: multiplying makes it bigger, dividing makes it smaller. If 9.3 ÷ 100 gave you 930, you moved the wrong way.
Going to a smaller unit → multiply. Going to a bigger unit → divide. A metre is bigger than a centimetre, so metres → cm means × 100.
LENGTH
MASS
CAPACITY
6.35 km → m   km is bigger, so × 1,000 → 6,350 m
950 g → kg   g is smaller, so ÷ 1,000 → 0.95 kg
Only length uses 10 and 100. Mass and capacity are always 1,000 — that alone is worth several marks.
A compound shape is just rectangles stuck together. Split it up, or start with the big rectangle and cut a piece out.

An L-shape: 12 cm wide, 9 cm tall, with a 5 cm × 5 cm corner cut out
Area = 12 × 9 − 5 × 5 = 108 − 25 = 83 cm²
Perimeter = 12 + 9 + 7 + 5 + 5 + 4 = 42 cm
Missing sides. The two horizontal pieces on one level must add up to the full width. Same for vertical. So: full length − known piece = missing piece.

Top is 12 cm, bottom is 7 cm → the missing horizontal step = 12 − 7 = 5 cm
Left is ? and the shape is 9 cm tall with a 5 cm step → 9 − 5 = 4 cm
Practise this in the Shape Lab tab — it generates a new shape with hidden sides every time you click.
Units: area is squared (cm², mm², m²), perimeter is not (cm, mm, m). Writing the wrong one loses the mark even when the number is right.
Read it twice. The second read is where you spot what it's actually asking for. Then follow four steps.

1. Underline the numbers and the units.
  2. Decide the operation. "altogether / in total" → add · "left over / difference" → subtract · "each / per / shared equally" → divide · "of" (as in 2/3 of) → multiply.
  3. Work it out, showing every line. Working earns marks even if the final answer slips.
  4. Answer the question that was asked — with the right unit, simplified.

A recipe needs 3/4 kg of flour. Maria makes 2/3 of the recipe. How much flour?
"2/3 of 3/4" → multiply
3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2 kg

A ribbon 9.6 m long is cut into 8 equal pieces. How long is each piece in cm?
"equal pieces" → divide: 9.6 ÷ 8 = 1.2 m
Question asked for cm: 1.2 × 100 = 120 cm
The classic loss: doing the maths perfectly and then giving the answer in the wrong unit. Re-read the last line of the question before you write your answer.

The 8 topics on your exam

Click a topic to open the rules, worked examples and the mistakes to avoid. Read one, then jump to Practice and drill it until you get 5 in a row.

name.en: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing fractions

text.en: Read topics 1–3 (comparing & simplifying, the four fraction operations, improper ↔ mixed). Practise each one.
Topics 4–5: multiplying & dividing decimals, then × and ÷ by 10 / 100 / 1,000. These are pure speed — go for accuracy first, then speed.
Topic 6: metric conversions. Learn the two chains by heart, then drill.
Shape Lab until you can find missing sides without help. Then word problems.
Full timed mock exam. Review every mistake, then re-drill only those topics.

html.en:
A 5-day plan to walk into that exam ready

Short sessions beat one long panic session. 30–40 minutes a day is plenty.

The 10 marks students throw away every year

  1. Forgetting to simplify the final fraction.
  2. Finding a common denominator when multiplying (you don't need one).
  3. Forgetting to flip the second fraction when dividing.
  4. Losing the decimal point: 12.6 × 4.3 has 2 decimal places in the answer.
  5. Moving digits the wrong way when dividing by 100.
  6. Multiplying when you should divide in a conversion (small unit → big unit means ÷).
  7. Writing cm instead of cm² for an area.
  8. Missing a side when going round a compound shape.
  9. Not answering the actual question in a word problem (it asked for mL, you wrote L).
  10. Leaving a question blank. Always write your working — it can earn marks.
The night before: don't learn anything new. Re-read the rule boxes in Learn, do 10 quick questions in Practice, then stop. Sleep is worth more marks than another hour of revision.

In the exam: do the sections you find easy first (usually multiple choice, powers of 10, conversions). Bank those marks, then come back to the shapes and word problems with the time you have left. Check every answer has a unit.

title.en: A 5-day plan to walk into that exam ready
